messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 4.5 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 5.5 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 4.5 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 4.5 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.8 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 60 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 60 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 120 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 4700 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 3300 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 60 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       3.33    3.36    49.3       -      5.05  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S2       3.18     3.2    44.2       -      10.1  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S3       7.08    7.13     110   0.209      5.01  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       2.21    2.22    33.8       -      1.04  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5        3.4    3.44    83.3       -       3.5  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S6       2.81    2.83    28.1       -       3.6  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 4.5 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a load $R_L$ from a piezo transducer.
    *   Output Requirements:
        *   $v_{avg} \ge 4.5\text{ V}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $v_{max} \le 5.5\text{ V}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $v_{pp} \le 0.05\text{ V}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{ s}$ (cold start)
        *   $dv \le 0.02\text{ V}$ (stability)
    *   Piezo Characteristics: $I_p = 40\text{--}120\text{ }\mu\text{A}$, $f = 80\text{--}100\text{ Hz}$, $C_p = 25\text{--}30\text{ nF}$.
    *   Open-circuit voltage amplitude $V_{oc} = I_p / (2\pi f C_p) \approx 3.8\text{ V}$.
    *   Reference Design (FBR) failed because $V_{oc}$ is too low to push the output to $4.5\text{ V}$ (it reaches $\sim 3\text{ V}$), and $V_{max}$ is exceeded in S3.

    *   Since $V_{oc} \approx 3.8\text{ V}$ and we need $V_{out} \ge 4.5\text{ V}$, a simple passive rectifier (FBR) is insufficient.
    *   We need a voltage boost.
    *   Two common techniques for piezo energy harvesting:
        1.  **SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor):** Uses a switch and an inductor to invert the voltage across $C_p$, effectively increasing the voltage swing.
        2.  **Boost Converter / Charge Pump:** Active switching to step up voltage.
    *   Given the available components (SYNC, S, L, C, D), a modified SSHI or a synchronous boost structure is possible.
    *   The SYNC controller can switch based on the piezo's peaks.

    *   *Concept 1: SSHI-like Inversion.*
        An inductor $L$ and a switch $S$ create an LC resonant circuit with $C_p$. When the piezo voltage reaches a peak, the switch closes, flipping the polarity of the charge on $C_p$. This increases the voltage amplitude seen by the rectifier.
        *   Configuration: Piezo $\to$ Bridge Rectifier $\to$ Storage $C_{out}$.
        *   Inversion circuit: A switch and an inductor in parallel with the piezo (or between the piezo and the rectifier) to flip the voltage.
        *   Actually, the standard SSHI flips the voltage *before* rectification.
        *   Proposed Topology:
            *   Piezo $pzp$ and $pzn$.
            *   Switch $S$ and Inductor $L$ in parallel with $pzp, pzn$ to flip the voltage? No, the switch needs to be in series with $L$.
            *   Wait, if I place a switch $S$ and inductor $L$ in parallel with the piezo, when $S$ closes, $L$ and $C_p$ resonate.
            *   But the SYNC controller allows pulses at peaks.
            *   Let's try: $L$ from $pzp$ to node $n1$, $S$ from $n1$ to $pzn$. When $S$ closes, $L$ and $C_p$ oscillate. This flips the voltage across $C_p$.
            *   Then, use a full-bridge rectifier (FBR) to feed $C_{out}$.

    *   *Concept 2: Synchronous Boost / Charge Pump.*
        Alternatively, a boost converter. But the SYNC controller is specifically designed for "piezo voltage extrema". This strongly suggests an SSHI approach.

    *   *Refining the SSHI-FBR (S-SSHI):*
        *   Piezo: $pzp, pzn$.
        *   Rectifier:
            *   $D1: pzp \to out$
            *   $D2: pzn \to out$
            *   $D3: 0 \to pzp$
            *   $D4: 0 \to pzn$
            *   Wait, this is a standard bridge.
        *   Inversion:
            *   $L1: pzp \to n1$
            *   $S1: n1 \to pzn$
            *   $G1: \text{SYNC}$, edges="both", phase=0.
        *   Storage: $C1$ on $out$.
        *   Zener Clamp: To ensure $V_{max} \le 5.5\text{ V}$, we might need a zener. $DZ33$ is $3.3\text{ V}$, which is too low (we need $4.5\text{ V}$). We can't use $DZ33$ to clamp at $5.5\text{ V}$. However, the system might be stable if $C_{out}$ is large and $R_L$ balances the power. Or we can use a resistor/capacitor combination.

    *   *Alternative Inversion (Parallel SSHI):*
        The bridge rectifier is connected to the piezo. The inversion happens across the piezo terminals.
        Components:
        - Rectifier (4x DSCH)
        - $L1, S1$ in parallel with the piezo.
        - $C_{out}$ on $out$.
        - $G1$ (SYNC) triggers $S1$ at both peaks.

    *   *Calculation for $L$:*
        $t_{on} \approx \pi \sqrt{L C_p}$.
        For $C_p = 25\text{ nF}$ and $L = 10\text{ mH}$, $t_{on} \approx 3.14 \cdot \sqrt{2.5 \cdot 10^{-7}} \approx 15.7\text{ }\mu\text{s}$.
        This is within the SYNC $t_{on}$ range ($10^{-7}$ to $10^{-3}$).

    *   *Potential Problem: Overvoltage in S3.*
        S3 has a very light load ($10\text{ k}\Omega$) and strong excitation ($120\text{ }\mu\text{A}$). This will charge $C_{out}$ rapidly. $V_{max}$ must be $\le 5.5\text{ V}$. Since we can't use a $5.5\text{ V}$ Zener (only $3.3\text{ V}$), we must rely on the storage capacitor size and the energy balance. Or a bleeding resistor.

    *   *Wait, can I use a Zener as a regulator?*
        No, $DZ33$ is $3.3\text{ V}$. The target is $4.5\text{--}5.5\text{ V}$.

    *   *Topology 1: SSHI + Full Bridge.*
        Components:
        1. D1: pzp -> out (DSCH)
        2. D2: pzn -> out (DSCH)
        3. D3: 0 -> pzp (DSCH)
        4. D4: 0 -> pzn (DSCH)
        5. L1: pzp -> n1
        6. S1: n1 -> pzn (ctrl: G1)
        7. G1: SYNC (ton=3e-5, edges=both, phase=0)
        8. C1: out -> 0
        *Wait*, the bridge orientation in the prompt: `["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]`.
        This means:
        - D1: pzp $\to$ out
        - D2: pzn $\to$ out
        - D3: 0 $\to$ pzp
        - D4: 0 $\to$ pzn
        Let's check current flow:
        If $V_{pzp} > V_{out}$, current flows $pzp \to out$ (D1).
        If $V_{pzn} > V_{out}$, current flows $pzn \to out$ (D2).
        Return paths: $0 \to pzp$ (D3) and $0 \to pzn$ (D4).
        Wait, if $V_{pzp} > V_{out}$, current must return to ground. If D3 is $0 \to pzp$, it's reverse biased.
        Correct Bridge:
        D1: pzp $\to$ out
        D2: pzn $\to$ out
        D3: out $\to$ pzp (No, that's not right)
        Let's use the prompt's suggested full bridge: `["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]`.
        Let's trace:
        $V_{pzp} > 0$ (peak): Current flows from $pzp$ through D1 to $out$, then through $R_L$ to $0$, then through D4 ($0 \to pzn$) to $pzn$.
        This works. D1 and D4 conduct.
        $V_{pzn} > 0$ (peak): Current flows from $pzn$ through D2 to $out$, then through $R_L$ to $0$, then through D3 ($0 \to pzp$) to $pzp$.
        This also works. D2 and D3 conduct.
        Okay, the prompt's suggested bridge is:
        D1: [pzp, out]
        D2: [pzn, out]
        D3: [0, pzp]
        D4: [0, pzn]

    *   *Topology 2: Half-Bridge SSHI (Simplified).*
        If we can't hit the $V_{max}$ or $V_{avg}$ with the full bridge, maybe a half-bridge with a capacitor? But we need $4.5\text{ V}$ and the piezo only gives $3.8\text{ V}$ peak. We definitely need the inversion (SSHI).

    *   *Topology 3: SSHI with a different inversion placement.*
        Instead of a full bridge, what if we use the SYNC switches to create a boost converter?
        Piezo $C_p$ $\to$ Switch $S1$ $\to$ Inductor $L1$ $\to$ Diode $D1$ $\to$ $C_{out}$.
        But SYNC switches are best for flipping $C_p$.

    *   *Checking the constraints again:*
        $V_{out}$ range: $4.5\text{ V}$ to $5.5\text{ V}$.
        $V_{oc} \approx 3.8\text{ V}$.
        The SSHI effectively multiplies the voltage. For an ideal flip, it can double the voltage. $3.8\text{ V} \times 2 = 7.6\text{ V}$, which is enough to overcome diode drops ($\sim 0.5\text{ V}$ total) and reach $4.5\text{ V}$.

    *   *Tuning the SSHI:*
        $L1$ value: $\sim 10\text{ mH}$ is a good starting point.
        $C1$ value: $\sim 1\text{--}10\text{ }\mu\text{F}$ to reduce ripple.
        $t_{on}$: $\pi \sqrt{L C_p}$. For $10\text{ mH}, 25\text{ nF} \to 15.7\text{ }\mu\text{s}$.

    *   *Refining the S3 $V_{max}$ issue:*
        In S3, $R_L$ is $10\text{ k}\Omega$ (very light). The power delivered by SSHI might be too high.
        $P_{in} \approx 4 \cdot f \cdot C_p \cdot V_{oc}^2$.
        With SSHI, $P_{in}$ increases.
        If $V_{out}$ exceeds $5.5\text{ V}$, we need to limit it.
        Wait, the prompt says I can use "at most 16 components".
        I could add a Zener diode $DZ33$ but it clamps at $3.3\text{ V}$, which is too low.
        I can't use a Zener for $5.5\text{ V}$.
        Is there another way to limit $V_{out}$?
        A parallel resistor (bleeder) could work, but it would waste energy and might make S4 fail.
        Let's first try the basic SSHI-FBR and see if the optimizer can find a $C_{out}$ and $L1$ that balances it.

    *   *Wait, the SYNC controller can be used for "pos" or "neg" edges.*
        For full inversion, "both" is correct.

    *   *One more check on the "Reference Design: FBR":*
        It failed $V_{avg}$ on S1, S2, S4, S6. (Needs $4.5\text{ V}$, got $2.2\text{--}3.4\text{ V}$).
        It failed $V_{max}$ on S3. (Needed $\le 5.5\text{ V}$, got $7.13\text{ V}$).
        This confirms that for S3, the power is already too high for the $10\text{ k}\Omega$ load, even with a simple bridge. SSHI will increase power further.
        This means I *must* find a way to limit $V_{out}$ in S3 while boosting it in S4.
        This is tricky. How to limit $V_{out}$ to $5.5\text{ V}$?
        If I use a Zener $DZ33$ in series with a diode? No.
        What if I use a SYNC switch as a shunt?
        If $V_{out}$ gets too high, we want to dump energy. But the SYNC controller doesn't have voltage feedback; it only knows the piezo's peaks.

        Let's reconsider the S3 case: $R_L = 10\text{ k}\Omega$, $I_p = 120\text{ }\mu\text{A}$.
        The FBR (without SSHI) already reached $7.13\text{ V}$.
        This means the load $R_L$ is simply too light to hold the voltage down.
        To lower $V_{out}$ in S3, we need more load.
        Wait, the $C_{out}$ value affects $V_{max}$? Not really, only the ripple and the startup time. $V_{max}$ is determined by the steady-state $P_{in} = P_{out}$.
        $P_{out} = V_{out}^2 / R_L$.
        If $P_{in}$ is constant, $V_{out} = \sqrt{P_{in} \cdot R_L}$.
        To reduce $V_{out}$, we need to reduce $P_{in}$ or $R_L$.
        Since $R_L$ is fixed for S3, we must reduce $P_{in}$.
        But the goal is to meet *every* condition.
        Wait, if the FBR already fails $V_{max}$ in S3, then *any* circuit that is *more* efficient than the FBR will also fail $V_{max}$ unless it has a way to limit the voltage.
        Is there a way to limit $V_{out}$ to $5.5\text{ V}$?
        Maybe a Zener $DZ33$ in a specific configuration?
        A $3.3\text{ V}$ Zener in series with a diode (say $0.7\text{ V}$) is $4.0\text{ V}$. Still too low.
        What if we use two $DZ33$ in series? $3.3 + 3.3 = 6.6\text{ V}$.
        A Zener clamp: $DZ33$ anode at $0$, cathode at $out$. It clamps at $3.3\text{ V}$.
        If we put two $DZ33$ in series (cathode of one to anode of the other), the clamp is at $6.6\text{ V}$.
        Let's try:
        DZ1: [0, n_z]
        DZ2: [n_z, out]
        This would clamp $V_{out}$ at $6.6\text{ V}$. Still higher than $5.5\text{ V}$.
        What if we use a $DZ33$ in series with a diode $D_{si}$?
        $D_{si}$ forward voltage is $\sim 0.5\text{--}0.7\text{ V}$.
        $DZ33$ (breakdown) is $3.3\text{ V}$.
        If we put them in series: $0 \to DZ33 \to D_{si} \to out$.
        The voltage at $out$ would be $3.3\text{ V}$ (Zener) + $0.7\text{ V}$ (Diode) = $4.0\text{ V}$ when the diode is forward biased.
        Wait, for the Zener to clamp, it must be reverse biased.
        $0 \to \text{Anode(DZ33)} \to \text{Cathode(DZ33)} \to \text{Anode(Dsi)} \to \text{Cathode(Dsi)} \to out$.
        When $V_{out} > 3.3 + 0.7 = 4.0\text{ V}$, the Zener breaks down and the diode conducts.
        Still not $5.5\text{ V}$.

        Let's think: how to get $5.5\text{ V}$?
        Maybe the optimizer can find a value of $L$ and $t_{on}$ that reduces efficiency in S3? No, that's not how it works.
        Maybe a large $C_{out}$ and a short simulation time? No, it's $0.8\text{ s}$.
        Wait, the FBR failed S3 with $V_{max} = 7.13\text{ V}$ and $V_{avg} = 7.08\text{ V}$.
        This means $P_{in} = (7.08)^2 / 10000 = 5.01\text{ }\mu\text{W}$.
        To get $V_{out} = 5.5\text{ V}$, we need $P_{in} = (5.5)^2 / 10000 = 3.02\text{ }\mu\text{W}$.
        We need to *reduce* the power harvested in S3 while *increasing* it in S4.
        This is the classic problem of a piezo harvester.
        But I have a SYNC controller. I can change the "edges".
        If I use "pos" instead of "both", I only harvest half the energy.
        $P_{in}$ would be $\sim 2.5\text{ }\mu\text{W}$ in S3, which would lead to $V_{out} = \sqrt{2.5 \cdot 10000} = 5.0\text{ V}$.
        This would satisfy $V_{max} \le 5.5\text{ V}$!
        But would it be enough for S4?
        S4: $R_L = 4700\text{ }\Omega$, $I_p = 40\text{ }\mu\text{A}$.
        $V_{oc} = 40\text{ }\mu\text{A} / (2\pi \cdot 100 \cdot 25\text{ nF}) = 2.54\text{ V}$.
        Without SSHI, FBR gave $2.21\text{ V}$.
        With SSHI and "pos" edges, we get a boost. Let's see.
        If we only flip at one peak, we still get some boost.
        Wait, "both" edges is standard SSHI. If we use "pos", we only flip every other cycle.

        Let's try two proposals:
        1.  **SSHI-FBR (both edges):** The classic approach.
        2.  **SSHI-FBR (pos edges):** To reduce power in S3.

        Wait, I can only propose 3. Let's try:
        1.  SSHI-FBR (both edges) - High power.
        2.  SSHI-FBR (pos edges) - Medium power.
        3.  SSHI-Half-Bridge - Maybe a different power profile?

        Wait, let's look at the $V_{avg}$ requirements again.
        S4 is the hardest for $V_{avg}$ ($R_L = 4700\text{ }\Omega$, $I_p = 40\text{ }\mu\text{A}$).
        $P_{load}$ for S4 at $4.5\text{ V}$ is $4.5^2 / 4700 = 4.3\text{ }\mu\text{W}$.
        FBR only gave $2.21\text{ V}$ (Power = $2.21^2 / 4700 = 1.04\text{ }\mu\text{W}$).
        We need a $\sim 4\times$ increase in power for S4.
        SSHI can definitely provide this.

        Let's refine the "both edges" SSHI. Maybe the $V_{max}$ in S3 can be handled by a large $C_{out}$ and the simulation time is short enough?
        $S3: P_{in} \approx 5\text{ }\mu\text{W}$. $P_{out}$ at $5.5\text{ V}$ is $3\text{ }\mu\text{W}$.
        Excess power = $2\text{ }\mu\text{W}$.
        In $0.8\text{ s}$, excess energy = $2\text{ }\mu\text{W} \cdot 0.8\text{ s} = 1.6\text{ }\mu\text{J}$.
        $\Delta V = \Delta E / C_{out}$.
        If $C_{out} = 10\text{ }\mu\text{F}$, $\Delta V = 1.6\text{ }\mu\text{J} / 10\text{ }\mu\text{F} = 0.16\text{ V}$.
        This is very small!
        So $V_{max}$ is not about the transient, but the steady state.
        The FBR result $V_{max} = 7.13\text{ V}$ for S3 means it reached steady state.
        So SSHI with "both" will definitely fail S3 unless we have a way to limit the voltage.
        But the only way to limit the voltage is to have a load that consumes more power.
        Since $R_L$ is fixed, the only other way is a bleeder resistor.
        But a bleeder resistor would hurt S4.
        Is there a way to use a SYNC switch to dump power?
        A switch from $out$ to $0$ triggered by the SYNC controller!
        If we have a switch $S2$ from $out$ to $0$, and it's closed for $t_{on}$ at "both" edges.
        $P_{dump} = V_{out}^2 / R_{on} \cdot (2 \cdot t_{on} \cdot f)$.
        $R_{on} = 2\text{ }\Omega$.
        If $V_{out} = 5\text{ V}$ and $t_{on} = 10\text{ }\mu\text{s}, f = 100\text{ Hz}$:
        $P_{dump} = 25 / 2 \cdot (2 \cdot 10^{-5} \cdot 100) = 12.5 \cdot 0.002 = 0.025\text{ W} = 25\text{ mW}$.
        That's way too much! It would kill the output.
        We need a much larger resistance for the dump.
